SAE features are derived from a pretrained sparse autoencoder and are not learned end-to-end for the steering task, limiting optimality.
Computational requirements are nontrivial for inference and scaling to larger models.
future_direction: Generalizing the framework to non-language attributes (e.g., tone, dialect)
Extending interpretability analysis to MLP contributions and other model families
papers.abstract: Deterministically controlling the target generation language of large multilingual language models (LLMs) remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in zero-shot settings where neither explicit language prompts nor fine-tuning are available. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, previously shown to correlate with interpretable model behaviors, can be leveraged to steer the generated language of LLMs during inference. Leveraging pretrained SAEs on the residual streams of Gemma-2B and Gemma-9B, we identify features whose activations differ most significantly between English and four target languages: Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, and French. By modifying just a single SAE feature at one transformer layer, we achieve controlled language shifts with up to 90\% success, as measured by FastText language classification, while preserving semantic fidelity according to LaBSE (Language-Agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding) similarity. Our analysis reveals that language steering is most effective in mid-to-late transformer layers and is amplified by specific attention heads disproportionately associated with language-sensitive SAE features. These results demonstrate the promise of sparse feature steering as a lightweight and interpretable mechanism for controllable multilingual generation.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Targeted Concept Erasure Tasks
papers.research_question: How can we develop effective evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) that measure their ability to disentangle concepts and remove spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs): an automated version of SHIFT and the novel Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric, which measure SAEs' ability to disentangle and causally isolate concepts.
papers.conclusion: SHIFT and TPP are effective, computationally efficient metrics for evaluating SAEs that can be applied to a wide range of datasets and show improvement during training, but they should be used as part of a broader evaluation suite due to their limitations.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT and TPP effectively differentiate between SAE architectures, with TopK and JumpReLU outperforming Standard SAEs.
Both metrics show improvement throughout SAE training, with most gains in the first 10% of training.
The metrics can be computed efficiently without an LLM judge, but using an LLM judge increases confidence and correlates well with the unfiltered versions.
The optimal sparsity for each metric differs, indicating a trade-off between sparsity and performance.
A single TopK SAE can achieve better performance on SHIFT than multiple Standard SAEs, as shown in the Pythia-70M experiments.
papers.limitation:
The LLM judge has a lower bar for interpretability than standard automated interpretability methods, potentially leading to false negatives.
The evaluation metrics rely on subjective hypotheses about human-understandable concepts, which may not reflect the model's true internal representations.
Hyperparameter selection and SAE latent selection are challenging due to lack of ground truth and variability across model sizes.
The metrics focus on causal isolation of concepts, but high-quality SAEs should also exhibit other characteristics like sparsity and disentanglement.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are an interpretability technique aimed at decomposing neural network activations into interpretable units. However, a major bottleneck for SAE development has been the lack of high-quality performance metrics, with prior work largely relying on unsupervised proxies. In this work, we introduce a family of evaluations based on SHIFT, a downstream task from Marks et al. (Sparse Feature Circuits, 2024) in which spurious cues are removed from a classifier by ablating SAE features judged to be task-irrelevant by a human annotator. We adapt SHIFT into an automated metric of SAE quality; this involves replacing the human annotator with an LLM. Additionally, we introduce the Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric that quantifies an SAE's ability to disentangle similar concepts, effectively scaling SHIFT to a wider range of datasets. We apply both SHIFT and TPP to multiple open-source models, demonstrating that these metrics effectively differentiate between various SAE training hyperparameters and architectures.

papers.title: Features Emerge as Discrete States: The First Application of SAEs to 3D Representations
papers.research_question: How do features in a 3D reconstruction model behave, and what learning dynamics explain their discrete state-like nature?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first application of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to 3D data, analyzing a 3D reconstruction VAE. It finds that the model encodes features as discrete states rather than continuous ones and provides a theoretical framework based on learning dynamics to explain this behavior and other observed phenomena like the bimodal distribution of transition points.
papers.conclusion: The work successfully applies SAEs to 3D data, revealing discrete feature representations and providing a framework of feature learning dynamics that explains the observed discretization and the counter-intuitive bimodality of transition points through a proposed mechanism of superposition interference redistribution.
papers.key_findings:
Features in the 3D reconstruction model Dora-VAE are discrete and state-like, approximating a discrete state space driven by phase-like transitions.
High-impact features have transition points that form a unimodal distribution centered around t≈0.5.
Low-impact features have transition points that form a symmetric bimodal distribution when aggregated across all features.
The model appears to redistribute interference from superposition to prioritize high-impact features, shifting the transition points of low-impact features.
Feature ablation and addition experiments demonstrate the causal relationship between specific features and the reconstructed 3D shape's position and structure.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on a single model (Dora-VAE) applied to 3D data and may not generalize to other models or domains.
future_direction: Validating observations across other domains (text, image) and models (PointNet++, LION).
Examining Dora-VAE with circuit detection techniques to see how features flow through the architecture.
Probing gradients of toy models to evaluate the proposed feature learning framework.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a powerful dictionary learning technique for decomposing neural network activations, translating the hidden state into human ideas with high semantic value despite no external intervention or guidance. However, this technique has rarely been applied outside of the textual domain, limiting theoretical explorations of feature decomposition. We present the first application of SAEs to the 3D domain, analyzing the features used by a state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction VAE applied to 53k 3D models from the Objaverse dataset. We observe that the network encodes discrete rather than continuous features, leading to our key finding: such models approximate a discrete state space, driven by phase-like transitions from feature activations. Through this state transition framework, we address three otherwise unintuitive behaviors - the inclination of the reconstruction model towards positional encoding representations, the sigmoidal behavior of reconstruction loss from feature ablation, and the bimodality in the distribution of phase transition points. This final observation suggests the model redistributes the interference caused by superposition to prioritize the saliency of different features. Our work not only compiles and explains unexpected phenomena regarding feature decomposition, but also provides a framework to explain the model's feature learning dynamics. The code and dataset of encoded 3D objects will be available on release.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
papers.research_question: Do commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones?
papers.core_contribution: Common SAE metrics (e.g., auto-interpretability scores) do not reliably distinguish between trained and randomly initialized transformers, indicating these metrics are insufficient for validating interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: High aggregate auto-interpretability scores alone do not guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered; the paper recommends routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics similar to those from trained models.
Standard SAE quality metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm) show similar trends across trained and randomized variants.
Token distribution entropy reveals that features from randomized models remain simple and token-specific, unlike features from trained models which become more abstract across layers.
The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for auto-interpretability tasks does not meaningfully discriminate between trained and randomized transformers in many settings.
Randomly initialized neural networks can preserve or amplify superposition present in input data, which may explain the similar SAE performance.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia models and the RedPajama dataset; results may vary with other architectures or data.
future_direction: Develop better metrics to distinguish between artifacts and genuinely learned computations in interpretability methods.
Investigate why randomly initialized transformers produce SAE metrics similar to trained ones, e.g., whether they preserve or amplify superposition.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: CytoSAE: Interpretable Cell Embeddings for Hematology
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied for interpretable morphological concept discovery in hematological imaging?
papers.core_contribution: CytoSAE is a sparse autoencoder that discovers interpretable morphological concepts in hematological images, generalizes across diverse and out-of-domain datasets, and enables explainable disease classification at patch, image, patient, and disease levels.
papers.conclusion: CytoSAE successfully learns interpretable morphological features across different hematological datasets, maintains generalizability to out-of-domain data, and enables multi-level analysis for interpretable disease classification.
papers.key_findings:
CytoSAE discovers morphologically relevant concepts that generalize across peripheral blood and bone marrow cytology datasets, validated by medical experts.
Patch-wise attribution allows sub-cellular level analysis of concepts, highlighting consistent morphological features across datasets.
Patient-level concept barcodes reveal disease-specific morphological features for AML subtypes, such as monocytic precursors for CBFB::MYH11 and granulated blasts for PML::RARA.
CytoSAE concepts achieve multi-class classification performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while providing explainability.
Ablation studies show the number of discovered concepts is stable across expansion factors and hyperparameters, with optimal layers between 7–11 for concept balance.
papers.limitation: Manual expert validation was conducted only at the dataset level, not per patient, to avoid human selection bias in concept discovery.
future_direction: Explore patient-specific concept retrieval while minimizing subjectivity.
Incorporate semi-supervised learning techniques to refine the discovered features further.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerged as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based foundation models. Very recently, SAEs were also adopted for the visual domain, enabling the discovery of visual concepts and their patch-wise attribution to tokens in the transformer model. While a growing number of foundation models emerged for medical imaging, tools for explaining their inferences are still lacking. In this work, we show the applicability of SAEs for hematology. We propose CytoSAE, a sparse autoencoder which is trained on over 40,000 peripheral blood single-cell images. CytoSAE generalizes to diverse and out-of-domain datasets, including bone marrow cytology, where it identifies morphologically relevant concepts which we validated with medical experts. Furthermore, we demonstrate scenarios in which CytoSAE can generate patient-specific and disease-specific concepts, enabling the detection of pathognomonic cells and localized cellular abnormalities at the patch level. We quantified the effect of concepts on a patient-level AML subtype classification task and show that CytoSAE concepts reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art, while offering explainability on the sub-cellular level. Source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/dynamical-inference/cytosae.

papers.title: Do Diffusion Models Learn Semantically Meaningful and Efficient Representations?
papers.research_question: Do diffusion models learn semantically meaningful and factorized representations of composable features, and how does training data affect this learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diffusion models undergo three distinct learning phases when learning to generate 2D Gaussian bumps, and that learning a semantically meaningful representation is key to performance. Moreover, even with imbalanced data, the learning of independent features is coupled, indicating that the model does not learn fully factorized representations.
papers.conclusion: The study observes three phases of manifold formation and finds that learning a semantically meaningful representation is essential to model performance. Moreover, models learn independent latent features in a coupled fashion despite imbalanced datasets, potentially indicating a coupled, less efficient representation.
papers.key_findings:
Diffusion models undergo three learning phases (A, B, C) with distinct failure modes.
Performance is highly correlated with the learned representation; formation of an ordered manifold indicates good performance.
Diffusion models learn semantically meaningful representations in the terminal phase, and the emergence rate depends on data density.
The learning process of independent concepts (x and y positions) is not fully factorized even under imbalanced datasets.
Models can compositionally generalize to some extent, as shown by training with incomplete data (hole in the manifold).
future_direction: Future investigation should look into the relation between learning and generation dynamics of diffusion models and their abilities to learn fully factorized representations and compositionally generalize.
The mechanism of how they generalize out-of-distribution warrants further investigation.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are capable of impressive feats of image generation with uncommon juxtapositions such as astronauts riding horses on the moon with properly placed shadows. These outputs indicate the ability to perform compositional generalization, but how do the models do so? We perform controlled experiments on conditional DDPMs learning to generate 2D spherical Gaussian bumps centered at specified $x$- and $y$-positions. Our results show that the emergence of semantically meaningful latent representations is key to achieving high performance. En route to successful performance over learning, the model traverses three distinct phases of latent representations: (phase A) no latent structure, (phase B) a 2D manifold of disordered states, and (phase C) a 2D ordered manifold. Corresponding to each of these phases, we identify qualitatively different generation behaviors: 1) multiple bumps are generated, 2) one bump is generated but at inaccurate $x$ and $y$ locations, 3) a bump is generated at the correct $x$ and y location. Furthermore, we show that even under imbalanced datasets where features ($x$- versus $y$-positions) are represented with skewed frequencies, the learning process for $x$ and $y$ is coupled rather than factorized, demonstrating that simple vanilla-flavored diffusion models cannot learn efficient representations in which localization in $x$ and $y$ are factorized into separate 1D tasks. These findings suggest the need for future work to find inductive biases that will push generative models to discover and exploit factorizable independent structures in their inputs, which will be required to vault these models into more data-efficient regimes.

papers.title: Data Whitening Improves Sparse Autoencoder Learning
papers.research_question: Does applying PCA whitening to input activations improve the interpretability of features learned by sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: PCA whitening significantly improves interpretability metrics of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a slight cost to reconstruction fidelity, by transforming the optimization landscape to be more convex and isotropic.
papers.conclusion: PCA whitening should be considered as a default preprocessing step for SAE training, especially when interpretability is prioritized over perfect reconstruction.
papers.key_findings:
Whitening transforms the SAE optimization landscape, making it more convex and isotropic, which improves feature recovery.
Whitening significantly improves interpretability metrics (sparse probing, SCR, TPP) for ReLU SAEs.
Whitening improves sparse probing for Top-K SAEs but does not significantly affect SCR or TPP.
Whitening causes a small but significant decrease in reconstruction quality (CE Loss and explained variance).
The benefits of whitening are more pronounced for ReLU-based SAEs than for Top-K SAEs.
papers.limitation: Experiments focus on middle layers of language models at the sub-2B parameter scale.
future_direction: Explore whitening's effects across different layers (early vs. late).
Investigate whitening on larger model scales (>2B parameters) and other architectures/modalities (vision, audio).
Study interactions between whitening and other training innovations (e.g., gated SAEs, transcoders).
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for learning interpretable features from neural network activations. However, the optimization landscape for SAE training can be challenging due to correlations in the input data. We demonstrate that applying PCA Whitening to input activations -- a standard preprocessing technique in classical sparse coding -- improves SAE performance across multiple metrics. Through theoretical analysis and simulation, we show that whitening transforms the optimization landscape, making it more convex and easier to navigate. We evaluate both ReLU and Top-K SAEs across diverse model architectures, widths, and sparsity regimes. Empirical evaluation on SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark for sparse autoencoders, reveals that whitening consistently improves interpretability metrics, including sparse probing accuracy and feature disentanglement, despite minor drops in reconstruction quality. Our results challenge the assumption that interpretability aligns with an optimal sparsity--fidelity trade-off and suggest that whitening should be considered as a default preprocessing step for SAE training, particularly when interpretability is prioritized over perfect reconstruction.

papers.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders scale to large models like Claude 3 Sonnet to extract interpretable features, and what do these features reveal about model behavior and safety?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can be scaled to extract interpretable, abstract features from Claude 3 Sonnet, revealing safety-relevant concepts and enabling model steering.
papers.conclusion: The method successfully scales to large models, providing insights into model internals and potential tools for safety, but further research is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders produce interpretable features for large models like Claude 3 Sonnet.
Scaling laws can guide the training of sparse autoencoders to optimize feature extraction.
Extracted features are highly abstract, multilingual, and multimodal.
Features can be used to steer model behavior, demonstrating causal influence.
Safety-relevant features related to bias, deception, sycophancy, and dangerous content are discovered.
papers.limitation:
The research is preliminary and caution is needed in interpreting safety-relevant features.
Sparse autoencoders have dead features and may not capture all concepts.
future_direction: Further work to understand the implications of safety-relevant features.
Improving sparse autoencoder training to reduce dead features.
Rigorous comparison of feature-based steering with other methods.
papers.abstract: Can sparse autoencoders scale to large models like Claude 3 Sonnet to extract interpretable features, and what do these features reveal about model behavior and safety? Sparse autoencoders can be scaled to extract interpretable, abstract features from Claude 3 Sonnet, revealing safety-relevant concepts and enabling model steering. The method successfully scales to large models, providing insights into model internals and potential tools for safety, but further research is needed.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Geometric Autoencoders -- What You See is What You Decode
papers.research_question: How can we avoid misleading visualizations in autoencoders due to distortions in the latent representation? The paper investigates a geometric perspective and a regularizer to mitigate such distortions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a geometric perspective on autoencoders, providing diagnostics (generalized Jacobian determinant and indicatrices) to visualize distortion, and a regularizer that minimizes the variance of the decoder's contraction, leading to more faithful embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The geometric autoencoder, combined with the proposed diagnostics, enables more faithful visualizations by reducing unnecessary distortions in the embedding, thus better capturing the data structure.
papers.key_findings:
The geometric autoencoder produces embeddings with more homogeneous contraction compared to vanilla autoencoders, as shown by the generalized Jacobian determinant heatmaps and indicatrices.
The proposed diagnostics effectively reveal distortions in autoencoder embeddings, such as the inhomogeneous contraction in vanilla autoencoders and UMAP autoencoders.
The geometric autoencoder outperforms baselines on a range of local and global metrics across multiple datasets.
The geometric regularizer is scale-invariant and works by minimizing the variance of the logarithm of the generalized Jacobian determinant.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes the decoder is an immersion (i.e., has injective differential), otherwise the pullback metric would not be positive definite.
The diagnostics are primarily designed for two-dimensional latent spaces, limiting their application to higher-dimensional latent spaces.
future_direction: Using parallel transport to create curved grids on the latent space that capture the intrinsic geometry of the dataset.
papers.abstract: Visualization is a crucial step in exploratory data analysis. One possible approach is to train an autoencoder with low-dimensional latent space. Large network depth and width can help unfolding the data. However, such expressive networks can achieve low reconstruction error even when the latent representation is distorted. To avoid such misleading visualizations, we propose first a differential geometric perspective on the decoder, leading to insightful diagnostics for an embedding's distortion, and second a new regularizer mitigating such distortion. Our ``Geometric Autoencoder'' avoids stretching the embedding spuriously, so that the visualization captures the data structure more faithfully. It also flags areas where little distortion could not be achieved, thus guarding against misinterpretation.

papers.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: Does neural network encode information in two complementary spaces: feature identity and feature integration?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides systematic evidence for dual encoding in neural representations, meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature integrations, and introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic evidence for dual-encoding spaces in neural network representations and introduces an architectural solution that achieves substantial improvements across multiple validation metrics, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors over SAE-only baseline.
The architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization with low squared norm features specializing in integration pathways.
Integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce statistically significant nonlinear interaction effects on model outputs.
Nonlinear integration components achieve 16.5% standalone improvement using only 3% of parameters, demonstrating parameter efficiency.
Sequential SAE+NFM approach shows 23.4% error reduction and 29.8% reduction in pathological KL divergence errors.
papers.limitation:
Scale constraints represent one primary limitation of this work. Our experiments on a 3B parameter model with 50k SAE features provide proof-of-concept evidence, but scaling to industrial-scale models with millions of features is likely challenging.
Integration interpretability presents ongoing challenges. While we demonstrated functional effects, these features remain largely opaque to direct inspection.
Limitations of traditional feature discovery approaches, as maximum activation analysis on secondary features failed to yield interpretable patterns.
future_direction: Dynamic analysis of how integration patterns evolve during training
Cross-model validation
Cross-layer analysis
papers.abstract: Current sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches to neural network interpretability assume that activations can be decomposed through linear superposition into sparse, interpretable features. Despite high reconstruction fidelity, SAEs consistently fail to eliminate polysemanticity and exhibit pathological behavioral errors. We propose that neural networks encode information in two complementary spaces compressed into the same substrate: feature identity and feature integration. To test this dual encoding hypothesis, we develop sequential and joint-training architectures to capture identity and integration patterns simultaneously. Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors. This architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization: low squared norm features contributing to integration pathways and the rest contributing directly to the residual. Small nonlinear components (3% of parameters) achieve 16.5% standalone improvements, demonstrating parameter-efficient capture of computational relationships crucial for behavior. Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Unsupervised Discovery of Semantic Latent Directions in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover semantic latent directions in the latent space of diffusion models in an unsupervised manner to enable controllable image editing?
papers.core_contribution: An unsupervised method to discover semantic latent directions in diffusion models using Riemannian geometry and the pullback metric, enabling controllable image editing without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: The proposed unsupervised approach successfully discovers semantic latent directions in diffusion models, providing insights into the geometry of the latent space and enabling semantic image editing without external supervision.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic latent directions found in an unsupervised manner lead to mostly disentangled attribute changes in generated images.
Editing in earlier timesteps (closer to T) changes coarse attributes, while editing in later timesteps focuses on high-frequency details.
The latent space X is a curved manifold, and spherical linear interpolation (slerp) is approximately geodesic, leading to smoother interpolations.
Global semantic directions can be found by averaging local directions and are consistent across different samples.
The method generalizes to Stable Diffusion, showing similar coarse-to-fine editing behavior in its learned latent space.
papers.limitation:
Entanglement between attributes due to dataset prior, e.g., the direction for long hair also converts male subjects to female.
Abrupt changes during editing in Stable Diffusion, possibly due to a more complex manifold or the influence of conditional guidance.
future_direction: Analyzing latent directions in conditions such as text prompts or segmentation labels.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of diffusion models (DMs), we still lack a thorough understanding of their latent space. While image editing with GANs builds upon latent space, DMs rely on editing the conditions such as text prompts. We present an unsupervised method to discover interpretable editing directions for the latent variables $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathcal{X}$ of DMs. Our method adopts Riemannian geometry between $\mathcal{X}$ and the intermediate feature maps $\mathcal{H}$ of the U-Nets to provide a deep understanding over the geometrical structure of $\mathcal{X}$. The discovered semantic latent directions mostly yield disentangled attribute changes, and they are globally consistent across different samples. Furthermore, editing in earlier timesteps edits coarse attributes, while ones in later timesteps focus on high-frequency details. We define the curvedness of a line segment between samples to show that $\mathcal{X}$ is a curved manifold. Experiments on different baselines and datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method even on Stable Diffusion. Our source code will be publicly available for the future researchers.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: Dissecting and Mitigating Diffusion Bias via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate social biases in diffusion models by identifying and manipulating the internal decision-making mechanisms (bias features) that causally drive biased outputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces DIFFLENS, a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies intrinsic bias features within diffusion models and enables fine-grained control over bias levels in generated content by directly manipulating these features.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel mechanistic interpretability approach to understand and mitigate bias in diffusion models, offering precise control over bias generation and insights into the model's internal decision-making processes.
papers.key_findings:
The paper identifies specific internal features (bias features) within diffusion models that causally drive the generation of biased content.
The proposed DIFFLENS method effectively mitigates social biases (e.g., gender, age, race) in generated images while preserving image quality and semantic coherence.
DIFFLENS allows for precise, fine-grained control over the level of bias in generated outputs by scaling or suppressing the identified bias features.
Different discovered bias features control distinct fine-grained aspects of generation (e.g., hair style for gender).
The method demonstrates effectiveness on both unconditional and conditional diffusion models across multiple social attributes.
papers.limitation:
The definition and evaluation of social bias are complex and inherently challenging, particularly for attributes like race, leading to potential instability in results.
The sparse autoencoder features may not fully align with human-interpretable concepts, as bias attributes are compound concepts that may relate to multiple features.
The approach treats debiased attributes as discrete categories (e.g., male/female), overlooking individuals who do not fit traditional classifications (e.g., non-binary gender or mixed race).
future_direction: Better alignment of sparse autoencoder features with human-interpretable concepts.
Addressing the representation of non-binary and mixed-race individuals in bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated impressive capabilities in synthesizing diverse content. However, despite their high-quality outputs, these models often perpetuate social biases, including those related to gender and race. These biases can potentially contribute to harmful real-world consequences, reinforcing stereotypes and exacerbating inequalities in various social contexts. While existing research on diffusion bias mitigation has predominantly focused on guiding content generation, it often neglects the intrinsic mechanisms within diffusion models that causally drive biased outputs. In this paper, we investigate the internal processes of diffusion models, identifying specific decision-making mechanisms, termed bias features, embedded within the model architecture. By directly manipulating these features, our method precisely isolates and adjusts the elements responsible for bias generation, permitting granular control over the bias levels in the generated content. Through experiments on both unconditional and conditional diffusion models across various social bias attributes, we demonstrate our method's efficacy in managing generation distribution while preserving image quality. We also dissect the discovered model mechanism, revealing different intrinsic features controlling fine-grained aspects of generation, boosting further research on mechanistic interpretability of diffusion models.

papers.title: Understanding and Steering Llama 3 with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we understand and steer Llama 3's behavior using sparse autoencoders to extract and intervene on modifiable features?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post introduces a desktop interface and method for interpreting and steering Llama-3-8B using sparse autoencoders, including training on chat data, automated feature labeling, and causal interventions via gradient attribution.
papers.conclusion: The release of this interface enables hands-on exploration of interpretability and steering techniques for Llama 3, demonstrating practical applications and setting the stage for future research in model understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Training SAEs on the LMSYS-Chat-1M dataset produces features more effective for chat applications compared to non-chat data.
An automated interpretability pipeline using Claude can generate human-readable labels for SAE features, with a contrastive scoring method to evaluate label quality.
A gradient-based attribution method using logit differences effectively surfaces intervention candidates for model steering.
Feature interventions can meaningfully change model output while minimizing performance degradation, but efficacy varies due to factors like cross-layer superposition.
SAEs trained on diverse data mixes tend to have more dead or low-frequency features, indicating trade-offs between feature diversity and training efficiency.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability pipeline struggles with influential features on special tokens or pivot points.
SAEs often find repeated 'echo' features due to L1 sparsity penalty.
Some features are difficult to intervene on effectively, possibly due to cross-layer superposition.
Training on diverse data mixes can lead to more dead and low-frequency features.
future_direction: Deeply understanding the tradeoffs of SAE architectural alternatives in practical usage.
Building interpreter agents for automated hypothesis testing and refinement of feature explanations.
Scaling up SAE training and investigating the science of SAE training data.
papers.abstract: How can we understand and steer Llama 3's behavior using sparse autoencoders to extract and intervene on modifiable features? This blog post introduces a desktop interface and method for interpreting and steering Llama-3-8B using sparse autoencoders, including training on chat data, automated feature labeling, and causal interventions via gradient attribution. The release of this interface enables hands-on exploration of interpretability and steering techniques for Llama 3, demonstrating practical applications and setting the stage for future research in model understanding and control.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: EigenFold: Generative Protein Structure Prediction with Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Protein structure prediction has reached revolutionary levels of accuracy on single structures, yet distributional modeling paradigms are needed to capture the conformational ensembles and flexibility that underlie biological function. Towards this goal, we develop EigenFold, a diffusion generative modeling framework for sampling a distribution of structures from a given protein sequence. We define a diffusion process that models the structure as a system of harmonic oscillators and which naturally induces a cascading-resolution generative process along the eigenmodes of the system. On recent CAMEO targets, EigenFold achieves a median TMScore of 0.84, while providing a more comprehensive picture of model uncertainty via the ensemble of sampled structures relative to existing methods. We then assess EigenFold's ability to model and predict conformational heterogeneity for fold-switching proteins and ligand-induced conformational change. Code is available at https://github.com/bjing2016/EigenFold.

papers.title: A Latent Diffusion Model for Protein Structure Generation
papers.abstract: Proteins are complex biomolecules that perform a variety of crucial functions within living organisms. Designing and generating novel proteins can pave the way for many future synthetic biology applications, including drug discovery. However, it remains a challenging computational task due to the large modeling space of protein structures. In this study, we propose a latent diffusion model that can reduce the complexity of protein modeling while flexibly capturing the distribution of natural protein structures in a condensed latent space. Specifically, we propose an equivariant protein autoencoder that embeds proteins into a latent space and then uses an equivariant diffusion model to learn the distribution of the latent protein representations. Experimental results demonstrate that our method can effectively generate novel protein backbone structures with high designability and efficiency. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/divelab/AIRS/tree/main/OpenProt/LatentDiff

papers.title: Demystify Protein Generation with Hierarchical Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Generating novel and functional protein sequences is critical to a wide range of applications in biology. Recent advancements in conditional diffusion models have shown impressive empirical performance in protein generation tasks. However, reliable generations of protein remain an open research question in de novo protein design, especially when it comes to conditional diffusion models. Considering the biological function of a protein is determined by multi-level structures, we propose a novel multi-level conditional diffusion model that integrates both sequence-based and structure-based information for efficient end-to-end protein design guided by specified functions. By generating representations at different levels simultaneously, our framework can effectively model the inherent hierarchical relations between different levels, resulting in an informative and discriminative representation of the generated protein. We also propose a Protein-MMD, a new reliable evaluation metric, to evaluate the quality of generated protein with conditional diffusion models. Our new metric is able to capture both distributional and functional similarities between real and generated protein sequences while ensuring conditional consistency. We experiment with the benchmark datasets, and the results on conditional protein generation tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed generation framework and evaluation metric.

papers.title: SE(3) diffusion model with application to protein backbone generation
papers.abstract: The design of novel protein structures remains a challenge in protein engineering for applications across biomedicine and chemistry. In this line of work, a diffusion model over rigid bodies in 3D (referred to as frames) has shown success in generating novel, functional protein backbones that have not been observed in nature. However, there exists no principled methodological framework for diffusion on SE(3), the space of orientation preserving rigid motions in R3, that operates on frames and confers the group invariance. We address these shortcomings by developing theoretical foundations of SE(3) invariant diffusion models on multiple frames followed by a novel framework, FrameDiff, for learning the SE(3) equivariant score over multiple frames. We apply FrameDiff on monomer backbone generation and find it can generate designable monomers up to 500 amino acids without relying on a pretrained protein structure prediction network that has been integral to previous methods. We find our samples are capable of generalizing beyond any known protein structure.

papers.title: Protein structure generation via folding diffusion
papers.abstract: The ability to computationally generate novel yet physically foldable protein structures could lead to new biological discoveries and new treatments targeting yet incurable diseases. Despite recent advances in protein structure prediction, directly generating diverse, novel protein structures from neural networks remains difficult. In this work, we present a new diffusion-based generative model that designs protein backbone structures via a procedure that mirrors the native folding process. We describe protein backbone structure as a series of consecutive angles capturing the relative orientation of the constituent amino acid residues, and generate new structures by denoising from a random, unfolded state towards a stable folded structure. Not only does this mirror how proteins biologically twist into energetically favorable conformations, the inherent shift and rotational invariance of this representation crucially alleviates the need for complex equivariant networks. We train a denoising diffusion probabilistic model with a simple transformer backbone and demonstrate that our resulting model unconditionally generates highly realistic protein structures with complexity and structural patterns akin to those of naturally-occurring proteins. As a useful resource, we release the first open-source codebase and trained models for protein structure diffusion.

papers.title: Accelerating Inference in Molecular Diffusion Models with Latent Representations of Protein Structure
papers.abstract: Diffusion generative models have emerged as a powerful framework for addressing problems in structural biology and structure-based drug design. These models operate directly on 3D molecular structures. Due to the unfavorable scaling of graph neural networks (GNNs) with graph size as well as the relatively slow inference speeds inherent to diffusion models, many existing molecular diffusion models rely on coarse-grained representations of protein structure to make training and inference feasible. However, such coarse-grained representations discard essential information for modeling molecular interactions and impair the quality of generated structures. In this work, we present a novel GNN-based architecture for learning latent representations of molecular structure. When trained end-to-end with a diffusion model for de novo ligand design, our model achieves comparable performance to one with an all-atom protein representation while exhibiting a 3-fold reduction in inference time.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Protein Structure Prediction with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Protein language models have revolutionized structure prediction, but their nonlinear nature obscures how sequence representations inform structure prediction. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a path to interpretability here by learning linear representations in high-dimensional space, their application has been limited to smaller protein language models unable to perform structure prediction. In this work, we make two key advances: (1) we scale SAEs to ESM2-3B, the base model for ESMFold, enabling mechanistic interpretability of protein structure prediction for the first time, and (2) we adapt Matryoshka SAEs for protein language models, which learn hierarchically organized features by forcing nested groups of latents to reconstruct inputs independently. We demonstrate that our Matryoshka SAEs achieve comparable or better performance than standard architectures. Through comprehensive evaluations, we show that SAEs trained on ESM2-3B significantly outperform those trained on smaller models for both biological concept discovery and contact map prediction. Finally, we present an initial case study demonstrating how our approach enables targeted steering of ESMFold predictions, increasing structure solvent accessibility while fixing the input sequence. To facilitate further investigation by the broader community, we open-source our code, dataset, pretrained models https://github.com/johnyang101/reticular-sae , and visualizer https://sae.reticular.ai .

papers.title: Structure-based protein and small molecule generation using EGNN and diffusion models: A comprehensive review
papers.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have revolutionized protein sequence and structure prediction. These advancements are built on decades of protein design efforts, and are overcoming traditional time and cost limitations. Diffusion models, at the forefront of these innovations, significantly enhance design efficiency by automating knowledge acquisition. In the field of de novo protein design, the goal is to create entirely novel proteins with predetermined structures. Given the arbitrary positions of proteins in 3-D space, graph representations and their properties are widely used in protein generation studies. A critical requirement in protein modelling is maintaining spatial relationships under transformations (rotations, translations, and reflections). This property, known as equivariance, ensures that predicted protein characteristics adapt seamlessly to changes in orientation or position. Equivariant graph neural networks offer a solution to this challenge. By incorporating equivariant graph neural networks to learn the score of the probability density function in diffusion models, one can generate proteins with robust 3-D structural representations. This review examines the latest deep learning advancements, specifically focusing on frameworks that combine diffusion models with equivariant graph neural networks for protein generation.

papers.title: ProT-GFDM: A Generative Fractional Diffusion Model for Protein Generation
papers.abstract: This work introduces the generative fractional diffusion model for protein generation (ProT-GFDM), a novel generative framework that employs fractional stochastic dynamics for protein backbone structure modeling. This approach builds on the continuous-time score-based generative diffusion modeling paradigm, where data are progressively transformed into noise via a stochastic differential equation and reversed to generate structured samples. Unlike classical methods that rely on standard Brownian motion, ProT-GFDM employs a fractional stochastic process with superdiffusive properties to improve the capture of long-range dependencies in protein structures. Trained on protein fragments from the Protein Data Bank, ProT-GFDM outperforms conventional score-based models, achieving a 7.19% increase in density, a 5.66% improvement in coverage, and a 1.01% reduction in the Frechet inception distance. By integrating fractional dynamics with computationally efficient sampling, the proposed framework advances generative modeling for structured biological data, with implications for protein design and computational drug discovery.

papers.title: Diffusion models in protein structure and docking
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative AI is rapidly transforming the frontier of research in computational structural biology. Indeed, recent successes have substantially advanced protein design and drug discovery. One of the key methodologies underlying these advances is diffusion models (DM). Diffusion models originated in computer vision, rapidly taking over image generation and offering superior quality and performance.
